title: Whitespace first, escapes last

blocks.text: The page's key point about escapes in a text block is the **order** of the compiler's steps: line terminators are normalized to `\n` first, incidental whitespace (and trailing whitespace) is removed second, and escape sequences are interpreted **last**. Until that last step, `\s` or a backslash at the end of a line is just ordinary characters.

Write `TextBlockContent.value(String raw)`. `raw` is the source between the opening `"""`'s line terminator and the closing `"""`: its last line is the whitespace before a closing delimiter on its own line, or the last content line. Return the text block's value. The JDK has one method for each step: `stripIndent()` does the first two, `translateEscapes()` the last.

headers: raw (`·` is a space, `⏎` a source line break)

cases.says: Indentation is removed and escapes such as \t and \" are interpreted.
Spaces before a \s survive, because \s is still two ordinary characters while trailing whitespace is stripped.
A backslash at the end of a line joins it to the next, whose indentation is already gone.
A \\ at the end of a line is one literal backslash, and the line break after it stays.
A written \r becomes a carriage return that is kept, while the source's own line endings become \n.

concepts: An explicit \r escape is kept, because escapes are processed after the source's line endings are normalized.
A \\ at the end of a line is one literal backslash followed by a line break, not a continuation.
A \ at the end of a line joins it to the next line, whose incidental indentation is already removed.
Escapes are interpreted after line terminators are normalized and whitespace is removed, so \s and a line-ending \ are ordinary characters until the last step.
\s becomes one space and fences the whitespace before it from trailing-whitespace stripping.
